analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for companies whose CEO pay exceeds 50 times the median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: after being introduced, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no action was taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise a large company's corporate income tax rate by 0.5 to 5 percentage points, depending on how many times larger the CEO's (or highest-paid employee's) pay is than the median worker's pay. A company paying its CEO 100 times the median would pay slightly more; a company paying 500 times or more would pay 5 percentage points more than the standard 21 percent rate. The tax applies only to larger firms — publicly traded companies, plus private companies averaging at least $100 million a year in gross receipts — and directs the Treasury Department to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio by replacing employees with contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large corporations with wide pay gaps, if the tax pressure pushes companies to raise median wages or narrow executive pay; the bill's supporters argue the tax savings or rate relief gives firms a financial reason to share gains more evenly. The federal government would also collect added revenue from high-ratio firms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at large corporations with wide pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: Corporations with a pay ratio above 50 to 1 pay a higher tax rate, rising in steps from 0.5 percentage points (over 50:1) to 5 percentage points (over 500:1), creating a direct financial penalty for extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps.
The ratio counts the CEO or, if higher-paid, the highest-compensated employee, so companies cannot avoid the tax simply by retitle executives.
The bill directs Treasury to write regulations preventing companies from manipulating the ratio by swapping employees for contractors or changing workforce composition.
Smaller businesses are shielded: private companies averaging under $100 million in annual gross receipts are exempt entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with very high executive-to-median pay ratios, which would pay up to 5 percentage points more in federal corporate income tax, and large private companies that would face new pay-ratio reporting requirements. If companies respond by cutting executive pay or raising worker pay rather than absorbing the tax, shareholders and executives bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large firms with big CEO pay ratios

drawbacks.text: The penalty is modest — at most 5 percentage points on top of the 21 percent corporate rate — so very profitable companies may simply pay the tax rather than change pay structures.

Large private companies with at least $100 million in average annual gross receipts would have to calculate and report a pay ratio under Treasury-set rules, a new compliance burden for firms that have never faced public pay-ratio disclosure.

Companies could respond in ways that raise the measured ratio reduction without broadly raising wages — for example, narrowing the gap at the top or adjusting workforce composition — rather than lifting median worker pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted nudge rather than a sweeping reform: it uses the tax code to penalize extreme pay gaps without capping anyone's pay or raising taxes on firms with modest ratios. The main honest concerns are that the maximum penalty is small enough that highly profitable firms might absorb it, and that the pressure could land on pay engineering rather than genuine wage increases. Against that, the compliance burden is limited to larger firms and the mechanism directly targets the pay-gap problem its sponsors identify.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on January 18, 2024, joined by Sens. Warren, Van Hollen, and Markey as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with very high CEO-to-worker pay ratios are better off, since the tax penalty never advanced and they face no rate increase. The Senate Finance Committee's inaction meant the proposal never reached a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High pay-gap corporations; the bill died in committee

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Excessive CEO Pay Act of 2024 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Sanders plus 4 of the Senate's 48 Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios
industries.note: The bill would raise their federal corporate tax rate by up to 5 percentage points unless they narrow executive-to-median pay gaps. Their financial interest in avoiding the tax runs against the bill's goal of lifting median worker pay relative to executive pay.

industries.industry: Large private companies ($100M+ annual gross receipts)
industries.note: They would face a new requirement to calculate and report a pay ratio under Treasury rules, though private firms under the $100 million threshold are exempt. The burden is compliance-focused rather than a direct tax unless their ratios exceed 50 to 1.
